standard.title: Representations of people and places across contexts
standard.description: analyse the representations of people and places in literary texts, drawn from historical, social and cultural contexts, by First Nations Australian, and wide-ranging Australian and world authors
standard.prior_knowledge: Students identify and explore ideas, viewpoints and issues in literary texts across historical, social and cultural contexts (AC9E7LE01). They have not yet analysed how representations of people and places are constructed — examining the choices authors make and what those choices reveal about context.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse how representations of people and places in literary texts reflect and are shaped by historical, social and cultural contexts, across First Nations Australian, Australian and world authors.

nodes.label: Representation as construction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that representations of people and places in literary texts are constructed — the product of authorial choices — not neutral or natural.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify two choices an author has made in representing a character or place and explain what those choices suggest about the author's perspective or context.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse how an author's choices construct a representation of a person or place, examining vocabulary, characterisation and narrative framing as constructed rather than transparent.
wider: Compare two representations of the same type of person or place (e.g. rural Australia, an immigrant community) from different time periods, examining how the construction differs

Examine how First Nations Australian authors construct representations that reflect unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing, and contrast with representations in mainstream Australian literature

response_modes.reason: The conceptual shift from 'the character is like this' to 'the author has constructed the character this way, and here's why' is a genuine hinge. Students resist this shift because it feels like it undermines the reality of the story. Wider cultural and historical contexts — particularly First Nations Australian authorship — help students see that representations are perspectives, not mirrors.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The First Nations Australian authorship context is explicitly foregrounded in the elaborations and offers educationally significant width. Representations that reflect 'unique ways of being, knowing, thinking and doing' challenge mainstream representational conventions and enrich students' understanding of what literary representation can do.
success_criteria: Student identifies authorial choices (not just character attributes) in the representation
Student connects at least one choice to a likely contextual influence (historical, cultural, social)
nodes.hinge_reason: The shift from 'the character is like this' to 'the author has constructed this character this way' is prerequisite for N2 — analysing how context shapes representation only makes sense if representations are already understood as constructed choices.

nodes.label: Context shaping representation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse how historical, social and cultural contexts shape how people and places are represented in literary texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Analyse one text and explain how a specific contextual factor (historical period, cultural background, social values) is reflected in the representation of a character or place.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse representations of values associated with key aspects (e.g. authority, community, family) in literary texts from two or more cultural or historical contexts, explaining how context shapes the representation.
wider: Examine how a recurring Australian motif (e.g. water, landscape, belonging) is represented differently across texts from different time periods, and what this reveals about shifting cultural contexts
Compare how First Nations Australian authors represent relationships with Country/Place in ways that differ structurally from how non-Indigenous authors represent natural settings
Analyse how the same historical period is represented differently by an author writing within it versus one writing retrospectively

response_modes.reason: Analysing how context shapes representation requires students to coordinate literary analysis with historical and cultural knowledge. The integration — using contextual understanding to interpret representational choices — is the core analytical capability this descriptor develops.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Cross-cultural and cross-temporal comparison of representations is the heart of literary study at Y9. The elaborations are rich with comparative directions. This node is where analysis moves from describing representations to interpreting them contextually — substantive and engaging territory.
success_criteria: Student analyses (not just describes) a representation, connecting choices to contextual factors
Student explains how the context makes the representation meaningful — why these choices make sense in this time/place/culture
